# Extraction method: eval, then AST, then regex

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-21 — added the rule to identify a binding by its
> checker symbol, and its spelling fallback where the global is undeclared.

Every extractor picks the least brittle method its source allows. The method
follows the SOURCE, not the author's habit.

1. **Eval or copy.** Ask the program for its own answer: run it, call tsserver
   or the TypeScript compiler API, import the module and print the computed
   object. When the source is JSON (a file, or a JSON block embedded in a
   binary), parse it with a JSON parser and copy it. Copy the whole value; take
   a subtree or normalize only for a named reader, never a 10% slice. This only
   breaks when the file or the anchor (a variable name, a key) goes away.
2. **AST.** When eval is not feasible: ast-grep, tree-sitter, Python `ast`. It
   survives code moving around as long as the shape matches. A pattern may
   wildcard what we don't care about (a string literal's wording, an argument we
   ignore); that is still the AST tier. Walk the typed nodes for the VALUES we
   do care about. Locating with AST and then running a regex over the matched
   code text to pull values out is the regex tier, not the AST tier. A regex
   over an already-decoded string value is fine.
3. **Regex.** Last resort, for prose or an already-decoded string that no parser
   can read. Each use carries a comment saying why tiers 1 and 2 cannot supply
   it, and a fixture a naive pattern gets wrong. A fact that measures a byte
   patcher's own matcher (Kiro's `rolloutPatchability`) is exempt: the matcher
   is the thing measured.

Locating a JSON block inside a binary with a short anchor pattern, then decoding
it with `json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode`, is tier 1. The anchor bounds the block,
the parser reads the value, and a missing bound fails with its own message.

## Rules

- **Support only the pinned version.** No legacy shapes, no fixtures for
  releases we no longer pin.
- **No field allow-lists in the extractor.** Copy what the source holds. When
  the shape changes, the hand-written reader that consumes the fact fails, and
  that failure is the design: fix the reader.
- **Fail when it cannot extract.** Never default, skip or count around a miss.
- **Identify a binding by its checker symbol, never by its spelling.** A local
  binding can shadow a global of the same name; when the checker cannot say what
  a binding holds, fail. A program without the global's declaration (no lib, no
  `@types/node`) resolves it to no symbol, so there a name the checker leaves
  unresolved matches the global by its spelling alone.
- **No layer between the extraction and its readers.** Readers are hand-written
  and read the copied value directly. Do not build a normalized meta format or
  automation that carries upstream changes up to them; when a reader breaks, an
  LLM or a person fixes the reader, and that is cheaper than the machinery.

Extractors write through the facts contract in `lib/extracted/` (see
`facts-contract.md`); do not add a per-owner loader.

## Settled — do not relitigate

- **Kiro rollout manifest, 2026-10-15.** The extractor in
  `packages/kiro-cli/lib/packaging.nix` matched each manifest entry with a regex
  against a fixed field list. 2.30.0 added `internal_treatment_percent` to
  `v3_prompt`, the regex missed it, and every update sweep held kiro-cli back
  from 2026-10-13 to 2026-10-15. The manifest was valid JSON the whole time.

# Extracted facts: the architecture

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-18 — Go owners run in-package extractor tests
> through the shared `goTestExtract`; shared reconciliation accepts single-key
> pattern rows. Every owner keeps one carried file; probes are not on the
> contract yet.

The contract (`facts-contract.md`, same category) is the spec: file shapes,
functions, failure kinds. This file is the why and the rules that keep the
machinery from growing back. Read it before adding anything under
`lib/extracted/`, `packages/<owner>/extract*/` or a harness's `lib/`.

## The pipeline

Five stages. Two of them take human input, and they are different inputs.

| Stage     | Lives in                                          | Written by                | Holds                                                                       |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| extract   | `packages/<owner>/extract/`, `passthru.extracted` | the extractor, in a build | one raw per system, carried into the forked `extracted/extracted.json`      |
| declare   | `packages/<owner>/extracted/facts.json`           | the extractor's author    | one row per key: type, source, which systems must carry it                  |
| decide    | `packages/<owner>/extracted/decisions.json`       | a human, dated            | ONLY how a key combines when systems disagree; absent when nothing diverges |
| aggregate | `lib.extracted.load` → `checks.extracted-index`   | evaluation                | the combined value per key; `index.json` for readers outside Nix            |
| annotate  | `packages/<owner>/extract/annotations.json`       | a human                   | what the extractor cannot measure: prose, dead-key reasons, refinements     |

`decisions.json` is not the hand-tuned layer. It answers one question, "these
two platforms disagree, which answer wins", and the drift check prints the exact
row to paste when that happens. The hand-tuned layer is `annotations.json`,
reconciled against the measurement by the owner's `rules.nix` so a stale hand
row fails the build. Owners without hand prose (Claude, Codex, glab, semble)
have no annotations file; owners measured on one platform (every owner except
Kiro and Codex) have no decisions file.

Reconciliation hand fields are non-blank prose. Owners may pass `patterns` for
repeated paths: `*` matches one key made of letters, digits, `_` or `-`. A
pattern matching no fact is stale; a fact claimed by multiple rows fails,
including overlaps between patterns and literal rows. The classifier stays in
`lib/redact/classify.nix`.

Go owners measure unexported structs and tables with a `_test.go` file copied
into the pinned source's package. `goTestExtract` runs it offline beside
`lib/extracted/go/nat_shared_test.go`, which holds the node type vocabulary, the
field walk and the output every Go owner shares; codec-specific typing stays in
the owner's test. CLIProxyAPI's `config` fact holds its v8 path-to-node mapping
as an opaque object because paths contain dots; CPA Manager Plus records
`config` and `environment` the same way. Their reconciliation readers consume
those facts for credential reasons. The owner fragments
`packages/cliproxyapi/docs/cliproxyapi-extraction.md` and
`packages/cpa-manager-plus/docs/cpa-manager-plus-extraction.md` describe each
extraction.

Consumers read the aggregate with `get` and `children`, at the place the value
is used. Nothing else reads a raw: the guard (`checks.extracted-contract-guard`)
fails any owner file that names `extracted/extracted.json` or `__platforms`,
reaches into `bySystem` or defines a combine.

## One file, carried per host

Each per-system extraction runs on a declared host, its derivation's `system`. A
static read of another platform's artifact runs on Linux and fills that
platform's side; only an extraction that must execute the binary runs on the
macOS runner, and it writes only Darwin's side. `regenerate` carries each host's
fresh raws into the one committed file. Only a carry from the base system,
`x86_64-linux`, makes the other systems follow every unforked node while keeping
their forks; any other host's carry leaves the rest exactly as committed, so a
difference new in its release becomes a fork that the next Linux carry keeps.
Following from both hosts would let each regenerate overwrite the other's side,
and no new difference could ever fork. Following from Linux is what keeps a
Linux bump evaluable: the per-system files it replaced let a Linux update
rewrite only Linux's raw, and every `equal` key a new release changed went
`divergent` against the stale Darwin raw. `get` throws on that at evaluation,
and `checks` forces every fact, so the Darwin regenerate that would have fixed
it could not evaluate (PR #2559, kiro 2.29.1 → 2.31.1, 2026-10-15).

Darwin CI's `extracted-facts` job therefore runs only owners with a `host-run`
row for Darwin, today Codex (clap help is compiled per platform).

## The subtractive rule

The seven migration PRs added +3300/−900 lines of code before two subtraction
passes (#2433, #2434) took most of it back. Every surplus line had the same
shape: a thing added "for completeness" that no reader needed. The operator's
standing instruction is that this machinery stays at the simplest form that
serves a named consumer. Concretely:

- **A fact needs a reader in the same PR.** A declaration no `get` or `children`
  call consumes is not declared. Measured data with no reader stays in the raw,
  undeclared: `load` lists it under `undeclared` and the index omits it, so
  declaring it is what makes it visible, and a reader is what earns the
  declaration.
- **An owner's `expect` row carries a value or a `contains`.** The lib accepts a
  presence-only need (`{ key = "..."; }`), and the fixtures keep that working;
  owners do not write one, because `get` already throws on a missing key, so a
  presence row is the same check written twice.
- **Measured once means no forks.** An owner whose extraction is the same on
  every host commits its Linux raw unforked, with `"systems": ["x86_64-linux"]`
  on every row; a Darwin host's own extraction is still compared with its
  projection. A fork whose sides are equal is a defect: `merge` never writes
  one.
- **No decision without a printed divergence.** A `decisions.json` row exists
  because the drift check failed `divergent` and printed it. An empty
  `decisions.json` is deleted; `load` treats absent as `{}`.
- **No wrapper over the readers.** Owner libs call `load`, `get` and `children`
  directly. A helper that re-shapes the aggregate for one owner is the first
  step back to per-owner merge logic.
- **Fixtures are the library's regression suite, not a mirror of owners.** Every
  combine, source and failure kind in the contract's closed vocabulary keeps one
  positive and one refusal case, whether or not an owner selects it today
  (operator, 2026-10-11: a combine with no current user is still part of the
  library). A fixture is deleted only together with the behavior it pins. What
  is NOT kept is a fixture for an owner-shaped scenario, such as a presence row
  or a second platform for a measured-once owner.
- **Delete in the PR that removes the last caller.** `mkExtractRegen`,
  `mkRegenerateExtracted` and single-mode `mkDriftCheck` outlived their last
  caller by three PRs because deletion was "a later batch". It is not.

## Settled — do not relitigate

- **Per-system raw files, retired 2026-10-15.** `<system>.json` per owner left
  each host free to rewrite only its own raw, which made every release bump a
  two-host race (PR #2559). Making `checks` lazy does not help: the rejected
  `lazyAttrsOf` probe still failed, because derived check names force every
  `ciPackages` entry. The fix is the single carried file.
- **Kiro's TUI is decoded, not materialized.** Its settings came from running
  the chat binary in a PTY until it wrote `tui.js`. The same payload is a zstd
  frame in the binary followed by its SHA-256 hex, which the chat binary accepts
  as `tui.js.sha256`; the static read matched the host-run facts byte for byte
  on 2.29.1 for both platforms (2026-10-15). Only the asset loader was not
  disassembled.
- **A hand-copied measured fact is a defect, not a backlog.** The 2026-10-10
  census counted 572 facts hand-copied into docs and tables, 281 with no feed.
  That number is a measurement of the problem, not a work list; the fix is a
  reader per fact only where a consumer actually depends on it.

## Probes: status and end goal

**Status.** `packages/delegate-routing/probes/delegates/<runtime>/` are run by
hand against a logged-in runtime. They write their own evidence files (including
`kimchi/extracted.json`, which is probe output, not an owner sidecar) and
nothing in Nix reads them. CI does not run them. The facts they establish
(delegation reach, nesting, hooks, worktrees, effort) are hand-copied into the
delegate-routing docs, which is the largest remaining source of the 572 above.

**End goal** (ASSESSMENT §6 of the private consolidation notes,
operator-approved as a direction; not yet scoped as work). Each probe meets one
of three fates:

1. A case that establishes a fact offline moves under the runtime's `extract/`
   and runs in CI as a `static` or `host-run` fact, with its darwin raw produced
   by the darwin leg when it is host-run.
2. A case that needs a login or the network stays operator-run and is declared
   `"source": "live", "systems": []`; its value is committed when the operator
   runs it and nothing in CI depends on it being fresh.
3. A probe with no declared consumer is deleted.

Consumers of probe facts (the delegate-routing skill, the capability map)
declare `expect` needs with values, so a runtime change under a skill surfaces
as a named failure. Until that lands, treat probe output as evidence to cite,
never as a fact source for Nix. The probe work owns the rewrite of this section.

## Where the rest lives

- `facts-contract.md`: the spec (same category, loads with this file).
- `typed-settings.md`: the generic option generator and render (same category).
- `dev/fragments/git-tool-settings/git-tool-settings.md`: annotations and the
  option generator for git-absorb, git-branchless, git-revise.
- `packages/kimchi/docs/kimchi-factory.md`: Kimchi's hand tables and reconcile.

# Extracted facts: the contract

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-18 — owners commit forked `extracted.json`; Linux
> carries make other systems follow; owner checks use `mkOwnerCheck`; Go owners
> extract with `goTestExtract` over the generic `goTest`; facts and
> reconciliation share the private redact classifier.

A fact is something the repo measured about a tool it packages: a settings key,
a model id, a hook trigger, a byte limit, whether a patch applies. Facts are
measured per platform, combined by declared rules, and read by consumers that
say what they depend on. This file is the contract every piece of that machinery
is written against. Per-owner code supplies data and an extractor; it never
contains merge, combine or platform logic. A check enforces that.

## Files per owner

| File                                        | Written by                               | Holds                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `packages/<owner>/extracted/extracted.json` | `regenerate`, on each host that extracts | every system's raw measured value tree, forked only where systems differ |
| `packages/<owner>/extracted/facts.json`     | the extractor's author                   | declarations: one row per key, type and source                           |
| `packages/<owner>/extracted/decisions.json` | a human, dated                           | exceptions: how a key combines when systems differ                       |

The aggregate is never committed per owner. `lib.extracted.index` writes it from
the inputs above; absent decisions default to `{}`.

`<system>` is one of `config/systems.nix`.

## The committed file (`extracted.json`)

One tree for every system in `config/systems.nix`. Where the systems agree a
value appears once. Where they differ, the smallest differing node is replaced
by a fork, `{"__platforms": {"<system>": value, ...}}`; a system absent under
`__platforms` lacks that key. Attribute sets are compared per key; any other
value, arrays included, forks whole. An owner measured on one host commits its
raw unforked, and every system's projection is that raw.

```json
{
  "rolloutFeatures": ["standalone_toolbox", "v3_prompt"],
  "rolloutPatchability": {
    "v3_prompt": {
      "patchable": false,
      "unmatchedSites": {
        "__platforms": { "aarch64-darwin": 2, "x86_64-linux": 1 }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

`lib/extracted/platforms.nix` (builtins only) owns the shape:

- `merge { "<system>" = raw; }` → the committed tree. Measured data holding the
  key `__platforms` anywhere, inside lists included, throws naming the path.
- `project merged system` → that system's raw. A fork mixing `__platforms` with
  other keys, a fork value holding `__platforms`, or a tree with no side for the
  system throws.
- `carry { merged; fresh = { "<system>" = raw; }; systems; }` → the committed
  tree with `fresh`'s sides replaced. When the base system `x86_64-linux` is
  fresh, every other system keeps its own fork values and follows the fresh raw
  at every unforked node, new and removed keys included, so a base bump
  introduces no divergence; a forked parent the fresh raw removes or retypes
  keeps the follower's whole committed value. When another system is fresh,
  every other system keeps its exact projection, so a new difference becomes a
  fork. When the base is fresh and some system is not, the base is the only
  fresh system; otherwise `carry` throws.

Nothing outside `lib/extracted/` and `checks/extracted/` reads the file or its
forks.

## Keys

A key is a dotted path into the raw JSON tree: `settingKeys`,
`rolloutFeatures.<name>.state`, `cli.commands.<name>.flags`. The segment
`<name>` matches any attribute name at that depth, so one declaration covers
every child and a new child inherits it. A path that names a list element is not
a key: a list is a leaf. Attribute names containing dots, such as those in
`settings.paths`, require an opaque `object` declaration for their parent.

## Declarations (`facts.json`)

```json
{
  "settingKeys": { "type": "set", "source": "host-run" },
  "rolloutFeatures.<name>.state": { "type": "string", "source": "static" },
  "rolloutUnmatched.<name>": {
    "type": "count",
    "source": "static"
  },
  "lastLiveRun": { "type": "string", "source": "live", "systems": [] }
}
```

| Field     | Values                                                        | Meaning                                                                                                                        |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `type`    | `bool` `count` `string` `set` `list` `object`                 | fixes validation and the default combine rule                                                                                  |
| `source`  | `static` `host-run` `live`                                    | `static`: same answer given the artifact; `host-run`: must execute on the host; `live`: needs a login or network, operator-run |
| `systems` | list of systems, default every system in `config/systems.nix` | which raws must carry a value for this key; `[]` for `live`                                                                    |

`set` is a list of strings compared without order. `list` is ordered. `count` is
a non-negative integer. `object` is opaque and only compared whole.

## Decisions (`decisions.json`)

```json
{
  "rolloutUnmatched.<name>": {
    "combine": "per-platform",
    "reason": "the patcher needs the host's own count; patchable is derived per host",
    "decided": "2026-10-10"
  },
  "models": {
    "combine": "intersection",
    "ignore": ["kiro-internal-preview"],
    "reason": "the option enum must be valid on both platforms",
    "decided": "2026-10-10"
  }
}
```

| Field     | Required | Meaning                                                                 |
| --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `combine` | yes      | one of the closed vocabulary below                                      |
| `reason`  | yes      | why; non-blank                                                          |
| `decided` | yes      | ISO date                                                                |
| `ignore`  | no       | set or list elements removed from every system's value before combining |

Combine vocabulary, closed: `equal`, `and`, `or`, `max`, `min`, `intersection`,
`union`, `prefer:<system>`, `per-platform`, `ignore`. Anything else is a
`bad-decision` failure. `and` and `or` apply to `bool`, `max` and `min` to
`count`, `intersection` and `union` to `set` and `list`, the rest to every type.
`ignore` as a combine drops the key from the aggregate entirely (it stays in the
raws). `per-platform` produces no combined value; consumers read per system.

Defaults when no decision row exists, by declared type:

| Type     | Default combine |
| -------- | --------------- |
| `bool`   | `and`           |
| `set`    | `intersection`  |
| `count`  | `equal`         |
| `string` | `equal`         |
| `list`   | `equal`         |
| `object` | `equal`         |

`equal` means the systems must agree or merge fails. That is deliberate: a
differing count or string is a decision, and the failure prints the row.

## `lib/extracted/facts.nix`

Needs only `lib`, like `reconcile`, so an option module can call it before
`pkgs` exists.

`declarations dir` reads the owner's required `facts.json` once for both `load`
and `hostRunOn system dir`. The latter selects owners with a `host-run` row
requiring that system, using the configured systems as the default for an
omitted `systems` field. The Darwin CI planner uses it without evaluating Darwin
checks on Linux.

### `load`

```nix
load {
  dir;                       # path: the owner's extracted/ directory
  secretHints ? {};
}
→ merge result
```

The only way to read raws. Reads `facts.json` and `extracted.json` (both
required: the absence of either throws when `load` is forced to weak head normal
form, naming the path) and `decisions.json` (optional, `{}` when absent), then
calls `merge` with every configured system's projection against every system in
`config/systems.nix`. A key a system's side lacks therefore fails as
`missing-system` for that system when its declaration requires it; a
declaration's own `systems` still narrows that. A fork's side for a system
outside `config/systems.nix` is never read.

### `merge`

```nix
merge {
  declarations;              # parsed facts.json
  decisions ? {};            # parsed decisions.json
  raws;                      # { "<system>" = <parsed raw tree>; }
  systems;                   # import ../../config/systems.nix
  secretHints ? {};          # passed to lib/redact/classify.nix per key
}
→ {
  aggregate = {
    "<key>" = {
      value;                 # combined; ABSENT for per-platform keys
      bySystem = { "<system>" = <raw value>; };
      type; source; combine; # as resolved
      failure;               # { kind; details; fix; } ONLY when value is
                             # absent because of a failure
    };
  };
  undeclared = [ "<key>" ];  # present in a raw, no declaration; informational
  failures = [ { kind; key; details; fix; } ];
}
```

`fix` is a ready-to-paste snippet: for `divergent` it is the complete
`decisions.json` row, keyed by the declared pattern, with every system's value
shown in `details`; for `declared-gone` it is "delete the declaration for
`<key>`". Pure evaluation cannot know today's date, so the generated row's
`decided` carries the literal placeholder `YYYY-MM-DD` and its `reason` is a
`TODO: <what to explain>`; `bad-decision` rejects both literals (a `reason` is a
placeholder only when, trimmed, it is exactly `TODO` or begins with `TODO:`), so
a row pasted unedited fails naming exactly the fields the human must fill.
`decided` must be an ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` date; its shape is checked, calendar
validity is not: the field is provenance, nothing reads it.

Failure kinds and when they fire:

| Kind                | Fires when                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `divergent`         | systems disagree and the effective combine is `equal`                                                                                                       |
| `missing-system`    | a declared key is present in at least one system but absent from another its declaration requires                                                           |
| `declared-gone`     | a declared key is absent from every raw; `missing-system` does not also fire. Not for `systems = []`                                                        |
| `type-mismatch`     | a raw value does not fit the declared type                                                                                                                  |
| `bad-decision`      | unknown combine, a combine its key's type does not take, blank reason, missing or malformed date, `ignore` on a non-collection, a row for an undeclared key |
| `undeclared-secret` | an undeclared key that `classify` flags as credential-shaped                                                                                                |

Not failures: an undeclared key (listed in `undeclared`); a key that only `live`
systems would carry; wildcard children appearing or disappearing. A wildcard
child present on one system and absent on another is a disappearing child, not
`missing-system`; the aggregate is keyed by concrete paths, one entry per
matched child, and `prefer:<system>` takes the only value when the preferred
system lacks that child. A declaration pattern never hides a raw leaf: a leaf at
a prefix of a declared path is undeclared and is classified like any other.
`ignore` as a combine drops the key from the aggregate only; its raws are still
validated and `type-mismatch`, `missing-system` and `declared-gone` still fire.

### `children` and `get`

`get aggregate "<key>"` returns the combined value. `get` on a key without a
combined value throws naming the key, the failure and the fix: the entry's
`failure` (for `divergent`, the paste-ready `decisions.json` row), or for a
`per-platform` key the advice to read `bySystem` from the index, or add a
`decisions.json` row that combines it. A key absent from the aggregate
(undeclared, or `declared-gone`) throws naming the key and both remedies. There
is no fallback value.

`children aggregate "<pattern>"` reads a declared key pattern containing exactly
one `<name>` segment and returns `{ "<child>" = <combined value>; }` for its
matching concrete leaves. Matching requires the same number of dotted segments,
with every fixed segment equal. Each value is read through `get`, so a matched
per-platform or failed leaf throws with the same key, failure and remedy. No
matches returns `{}`: disappearing wildcard children are not a failure. A
pattern without exactly one `<name>` segment throws. Consumers use these readers
to read facts.

### `expect`

```nix
expect {
  aggregate;
  consumer = "delegate-routing";   # named in every failure
  needs = [
    { key = "tools"; contains = "invoke_sub_agent"; }
    { key = "steering.maxChars"; value = 50000; }
    { key = "hookTriggers"; }      # presence only
  ];
}
→ { failures = [ { kind = "expectation"; consumer; key; expected; actual; } ]; }
```

A consumer declares the facts its generated output was written against. When the
aggregate no longer satisfies a need, the consumer's own check fails, naming the
consumer, the key, the expected and the actual value. This is how "the harness
changed under the skill" surfaces.

### `index`

Needs `pkgs`. Takes `{ "<owner>" = merge-result; }` and writes one JSON per
owner plus `index.json` across owners, each key carrying `value`, `bySystem`,
`type`, `source`, `combine`. External readers (skills, CI scripts) read these
files; Nix consumers read the aggregate directly.

`checks.extracted-index` and the Darwin CI planner load the explicit
logical-name-to-directory map in `checks/extracted/owners.nix`. These names
identify its JSON files and index keys independently of owner directory names.
External readers build that attribute and read its files.

## Drift

`mkOwnerCheck { dir; name; package ? null; extracted ? { <host> = package.passthru.extracted; }; needs ? []; results ? {}; }`
in `lib/extracted/default.nix` loads an owner's facts, checks its optional
consumer needs and supplied annotation `results`, and compares each extraction.
`results.facts` and `results.consumers` are the builder's own surfaces; a
`results` that names either is refused, so a supplied `facts.failures = []` can
never silence a merge failure. `dir` names the committed facts directory; `name`
identifies the check and its `packages/<name>/extracted/extracted.json`
regeneration path, independently of that directory's physical location. An owner
whose extractions run on another host passes `extracted` itself: Kiro reads both
releases statically on Linux.

`mkDriftCheck { committed; extracted; name; results ? {}; sidecar; }` takes the
committed `extracted.json` as a path, its repository path as a string, and
`extracted = { "<system>" = derivation; }`. A derivation's `system` is the host
its extraction runs on. On host `S` the check compares every system whose
extraction runs on `S` with that system's projection of the committed file; a
static extractor may supply several systems, a host-run one only `S`, and a host
that runs none compares nothing. Every drifted system is reported, each naming
its side of the committed file, and the check fails once at the end.

Owner checks expose `passthru.regenerate`: run
`nix run .#checks.<host>.<name>-extracted.passthru.regenerate` from the
repository root to `carry` every extraction this host runs into the committed
file, format it, set its mode to 0644 and report the written path. A host that
runs every system's extraction rewrites the file from fresh raws alone. Linux
carries the other systems forward at every unforked node, and their own host's
check then validates their projection; any other host rewrites only its own
side, forming a fork wherever it now differs.

Owner update scripts use `regenCommand { name; }` to build and run that
regenerator on the current host.

A Go owner's `passthru.extracted` is
`goTestExtract { package; packagePath; testFile; }`: through `goTest` it joins
`testFile` and `go/nat_shared_test.go` (given the test's package clause) to
`packagePath` under the buildGoModule `package`'s `modRoot`, runs
`TestNatExtract` offline with the package's toolchain and vendor tree, and keeps
the object of surfaces the test writes to `$NAT_EXTRACT_OUT`.

## The guard

`checks.extracted-contract-guard` fails when any tracked file outside
`lib/extracted/` and `checks/extracted/` names `extracted/extracted.json` or
`__platforms`, reaches into `bySystem`, or defines a combine. Owners supply data
and extractors only.

## Fixtures (`checks/extracted/facts.nix`)

Eval-time cases in the style of `checks/extracted/reconcile.nix`, each naming
its refused input or its visible result, plus one derivation that asserts the
`divergent` message contains the paste-ready row.

1. Two systems agree: aggregate carries the value, no failures.
2. Differ with a rule: `set` intersection by default; `bool` and; `count` with a
   `max` or `min` decision; `bool` with `or`; `string` with
   `prefer:x86_64-linux`.
3. Differ without a rule: `divergent`, and `fix` is a complete decisions row.
4. New key, undeclared, not secret-shaped: no failure, listed in `undeclared`.
5. New key, undeclared, secret-shaped: `undeclared-secret`.
6. Declared key absent everywhere: `declared-gone`.
7. Type mismatch: a string where `count` is declared.
8. `per-platform`: no combined value; `get` throws with the reader remedy.
9. `expect`: a satisfied set and a failed set, failure names the consumer.
10. Wildcard declaration applies to every child, and a new child is covered. A
    disappearing child keeps its sole value even when the preferred system lacks
    it.
11. `bad-decision`: unknown combine; blank reason; row for an undeclared key.
12. `ignore` removes an element before intersection.
13. `missing-system`: declared for both, present in one.
14. `live` with `systems = []`: no system required, no failure; `get` on a
    divergent key throws and the entry carries merge's failure, and
    `extracted-facts-divergent-fix` evaluates that `get` in a dummy-store
    `nix-instantiate` to assert its message names the key and the row.
15. `load` (fixture directories under `checks/extracted/load/`): a key forked
    across both configured systems and one outside `config/systems.nix` (never
    read) merges clean with its decision applied; with Darwin's side lacking
    every key, each declared key fails `missing-system` naming it, and a
    `prefer:aarch64-darwin` decision is not a `bad-decision`. `load` on a
    directory without `facts.json`, or without `extracted.json`, throws. An
    unforked file whose declarations require only Linux loads without failures.
    A committed file with a fork, carried by a fresh Linux raw that adds a
    feature, loads clean and Darwin's projection holds the feature and keeps its
    fork; replacing only Linux's side instead fails `divergent`.

`checks/extracted/platforms.nix` pins the committed file: agreement stored once,
the smallest differing node forked, arrays forked whole, a key one system lacks,
a single raw left unforked, the merge/project round trip, the sentinel refused
in measured data (lists included) and in malformed forks, and `carry` following,
dropping, collapsing a fork, merging when every system is fresh, keeping a
removed or retyped forked parent whole, a Darwin carry leaving Linux as
committed and forming the fork a later Linux carry keeps, and refusing two fresh
systems while another is not.

`checks/extracted/drift.nix` runs `mkDriftCheck`'s script per case: a fork is
compared through the host's projection, a foreign-system extraction is skipped,
and every drifted system is named while a matching one is not. A case with
`regenerate` also reads the regenerate script's text, which must name each fresh
raw this host carries and omit the foreign one.

# Extracted facts: typed settings and their render

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-21 — `lib/extracted/options.nix` types the
> CLIProxyAPI and CPA Manager Plus node trees with nullable container children
> and `secretFile` nodes, and refuses a refinement row that would apply on a
> node with a secret or secret-file descendant; `render.nix` lifts secrets and
> secret files into `{$NAME}` placeholders and refuses a malformed `_redact`
> marker; `goTest` runs each owner's loader check.

Two owners, CLIProxyAPI and CPA Manager Plus, get typed settings from their
reconciled facts through one generator. The four older generators
(`packages/claude-code/lib/generateSettingsOptions.nix`,
`packages/kimchi/lib/extracted.nix`, `packages/glab/lib/schema.nix`,
`lib/git-tool-settings/`) predate it and each carry their own scalar switch,
null rule and hand tables. Moving them onto it is separate work; do not add a
fifth.

## The generator (`lib/extracted/options.nix`)

Input is one surface's reconciled entries, `(reconcile …).<surface>.entries`:
path → node in the Go extractors' grammar (`.` between keys, `[]` for a list
element, `.<name>` for a map value). It needs only `lib`.

- Every option is `nullOr T` with `default = null`; null drops the key, so the
  tool's own default applies. Objects are closed submodules; a list is
  `listOf (nullOr T)` for its `[]` node, a map `attrsOf (nullOr T)` for its
  `.<name>` node. Null list elements and map values are accepted and dropped by
  the render.
- `bool`, `int`, `number`, `string` map to the obvious types; `enum` on a node
  gives `types.enum`; `duration` is `strMatching` time.ParseDuration's grammar;
  `any` is a JSON value (the type of `pkgs.formats.json`), and its child nodes
  are consumed by it.
- A node carrying `secret` (the reason an annotations.json row gives, which
  reconcile requires for every classifier hit) is
  `nullOr redact.types.redacted`, including list elements and map values. Its
  non-null type accepts references only. No refinement row widens a secret: a
  row on one is reported stale, and a row that would apply on any node with a
  secret or secret-file descendant fails evaluation, naming both paths, because
  the row returns the whole value type and would replace the redacted
  descendant.
- A node carrying `secretFile` (a reason, like `secret`) is
  `nullOr redact.types.secretFile`, delivered as a file path
  (`dev/fragments/redact/redact.md`, Secret files). It marks a key file the tool
  reads, such as `adminKeyFile`, never a path it writes, such as `dataKeyPath`.
  A node with both fields fails evaluation; a refinement row on one is stale.
- Node fields it does not read fail evaluation unless the owner lists them in
  `unread`, so an extractor that learns a fact must teach the generator.

Owner tables, keyed by path: `exclusions` (path → reason; no option) and
`refinements` (path → `{ type; refine; }`, applied only while the node still has
the `type` the row was written for). `report` lists `staleExclusions`,
`staleRefinements`, `untyped` (a type or a list/map with no element node that
nothing maps) and `misplaced` (a node whose parent is missing or cannot hold
it); every list is empty for a current owner.

`sample { overrides; }` sets every leaf from its node: `true`, `1`, `1.5`,
`"sample"`, `"1s"`, the first enum value, one list element, one map entry
`sample`, a dummy `redact.file` for a secret or a secret file. An override names
a node path and replaces that value; one naming no node fails.

## The render (`lib/extracted/render.nix`)

`render { prefix; settings; }` returns `{ content; secrets; }`. Nulls are
dropped recursively, inside lists too. Each redact reference becomes the whole
JSON string `"{$<PREFIX>_<PATH>}"`, the env-reference token
`lib/ai/mcpProxy.nix` writes into its Caddyfile, and `secrets` maps that name to
the reference; a secret-file value keeps its tag there, so the launcher fills
its placeholder with a path. Lifting uses `redact.isRedacted` and
`redact.isAsFile`, never a test of its own. Any other set with a `_redact` key
(`redact.isReserved`, after nulls are dropped), even in untyped JSON such as
CLIProxyAPI's `plugins.configs`, is refused through `redact.sealed`. Two paths
that sanitize to one name fail evaluation.

`content` is JSON text for both owners, YAML included: JSON is YAML 1.2, and
CLIProxyAPI's yaml.v3 loader reads it (its loader check proves it). One quoting
means one substitution rule for a launcher: replace the quoted token with the
value encoded as a JSON string. `fill` is that rule in Nix, for checks.

Why not `pkgs.formats.yaml`/`json` (tried 2026-10-18): `generate` yields a
derivation, so the text is only reachable through import-from-derivation, and
its YAML writer single-quotes `'{$NAME}'`, which would give YAML a second escape
rule.

## Loader checks

`goTest { env; name; package; packagePath; postTest; run; sources; }` in
`lib/extracted/default.nix` joins `sources` to a Go package of a buildGoModule
source and runs one test offline; `goTestExtract` is it with the shared
extractor file. Each owner's `<owner>-settings` check evaluates `sample` through
`settingsType`, renders it, fills each placeholder with a dummy that needs JSON
escapes, and runs an in-package `settings_test.go` against the tool's own
loader. `checks.extracted-options` covers the generator and render on fixtures
and requires every owner exporting `settingsType` to report empty.
